content: The Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) provides a comprehensive dataset known as the PRAMS Automated Research File (ARF). Detailed instructions on how to request access to this data are available. PRAMS data has been utilized by the CDC and its partners to implement initiatives aimed at improving maternal and child health outcomes. These efforts are highlighted in success stories that demonstrate the practical application of PRAMS data. Between 2016 and 2021, PRAMS collected data on selected maternal and child health indicators. This information is available for review and analysis. The PRAMS program includes several key resources: Overview of PRAMS: A foundational explanation of the PRAMS program, including frequently asked questions. Special Research Projects: PRAMS conducts specialized studies to address specific maternal and child health issues. Data Methodology: Detailed descriptions of the methodologies used to collect and analyze PRAMS data. PRAMS Questionnaires: Information on the structure and content of PRAMS questionnaires, including examples from previous years. Participating Sites: A list of U.S. states and territories involved in PRAMS surveillance, along with contact information. PRAMS Publications: Links to journal articles and other publications that utilize PRAMS data. Additional resources related to maternal and child health include: Division of Reproductive Health: This division focuses on reproductive, maternal, and infant health. National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities (NCBDDD): This center works to improve the health of vulnerable populations, including those affected by birth defects and developmental disabilities. Division of Nutrition, Physical Activity, and Obesity: This division addresses issues related to nutrition, physical activity, and obesity, with a focus on public health impact. Maternal and Child Health Epidemiology Program (MCHEP): This program outlines its mission, goals, and activities aimed at improving maternal and child health through epidemiological research. Association of Maternal and Child Health Programs (AMCHP): A resource for maternal and child health professionals. Health Resources and Services Administration, Maternal and Child Health Bureau: A federal agency dedicated to improving health outcomes for mothers and children. National Healthy Start: A program designed to reduce infant mortality and improve maternal health. March of Dimes: An organization focused on preventing birth defects, premature birth, and infant mortality. Tribal Epidemiology Centers: Centers that provide epidemiological support to tribal communities.
